recorded: 11 April 1950, Columbia 30th Street Studio, New York
intro: Robert Casadesus plays Debussy’s cakewalk, a dry, springy dance with an unexpected guest: Wagner’s Tristan. The grand romantic phrase arrives “with great emotion” and gets a cheeky answer.

sections.label: A · The E♭-major dance
sections.mNote: Syncopations jostle a steady bass-and-chord accompaniment

sections.label: B · Tristan at the dance
sections.mNote: Wagner’s phrase meets clipped grace-note replies

sections.label: A′ · The cakewalk returns
sections.mNote: The first tempo and E♭-major syncopations return

cues.title: A dance with elbows
cues.text: The tune pushes its accents across the beat while the left hand keeps up a regular bass-and-chord step. Debussy marks it très net et très sec — very clear and very dry. Sudden loud notes poke through the quieter ones.
cues.evidence: Debussy, Children’s Corner, Durand (1908), plate D. & F. 7188, pp. 24–25: syncopation, bass-and-chord accompaniment, contrasting dynamics and très net et très sec. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0d/IMSLP252526-PMLP02387-Debussy%2C_Claude-Childrens_Corner_Durand_7188_filter.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dancers and a racist doll
cues.text: In Paris in 1902–03, seven African American women, the Florida Creole Girls, help make the cakewalk a craze. Debussy’s title names a racist caricature: Florence Kate Upton’s blackface doll, introduced in an 1895 picture book.
cues.evidence: James Deaville, Debussy’s Cakewalk (2014), on the Florida Creole Girls at the Casino de Paris: https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol2-n1/debussy-s-cakewalk/. David Pilgrim, Jim Crow Museum, on Upton’s 1895 character and minstrel doll: https://jimcrowmuseum.ferris.edu/golliwog/homepage.htm.

cues.title: Tristan gets an answer
cues.text: The slower middle quotes the opening of Wagner’s Tristan und Isolde. Debussy writes avec une grande émotion — with great emotion — above the yearning phrase. Short, clipped chords answer it, as if the pianist has just remembered where the dance floor is.
cues.evidence: Durand score, pp. 26–27: avec une grande émotion and the alternating chromatic phrase and grace-note chords. The Tristan quotation is discussed by Deaville in Debussy’s Cakewalk (2014).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Back to the cakewalk
cues.text: The first tempo snaps back, with E♭ major and the familiar bass-and-chord step. The tune recovers its sharp elbows. Near the end, Debussy lets it dwindle to little fragments before two fortissimo chords shut the door.
cues.evidence: Durand score, pp. 27–28: 1° Tempo, restored three-flat signature and dance, quiet fragments, and two final detached fortissimo chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The dance slows into G♭ major
transitions.how: The E♭-major dance dwindles to small replies between the hands. Six flats replace three, and Un peu moins vite slows the pace. Over repeated bass notes, grace-note chords introduce the G♭-major middle; soon the piano stretches out into the chromatic phrase from Tristan.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, pp. 25–26: change to six flats, Un peu moins vite, repeated bass and grace-note chords, followed by the Tristan quotation.

transitions.title: The bass puts the dance back
transitions.how: The middle slows under Retenez and Toujours retenu. A short descending line is left alone before a breath mark. Then 1° Tempo restores E♭ major and the left hand’s bass-and-chord accompaniment; the right hand resumes its syncopated dance.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, p. 27: Retenez, Toujours retenu, unaccompanied descending phrase, breath mark, three-flat signature and 1° Tempo.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The solo pianist is identified on the carrier, repository record and official discography. No other performer is claimed.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The original work is for solo piano. The particular performing edition used by Casadesus is not identified; the viewed Durand score is study evidence, not evidence that this exact copy or impression was used. Section boundaries are score-informed passage estimates, not bar alignments.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The official discography identifies 11 April 1950 for Children’s Corner and includes ML 4366 in the issue list. The LP’s 1951 publication and the 2022 transfer are separate dates.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Columbia 30th Street Studio, New York, United States
fields.note: Venue and city are stated in the dated suite row; they are not inferred from the record company’s location.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The transferred carrier is a 12-inch vinyl LP; Debussy is on its second side.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: ML 4366 (sleeve and library catalogue); ML 54366 (scanned disc label)
fields.note: Both forms occur in the evidence. The library dates the ML 4366 issue to 1951; the exact pressing date of the scanned ML 54366-labelled copy is not established. No explanation for the number variation is invented.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: The side matrix is printed on the Debussy label. Individual session take and stamper identifiers are not established; the side matrix is not presented as a session take number.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The explicit ripping_operator credit is used. The separate catalogue/scanning operator and uploader are not substituted for the audio transfer operator.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: Item ripping_date is 20220321012946. This is the transfer date, not the 1950 session, 1951 LP issue, scan date or repository added date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Technics SL1200MK5 turntable + Audio-Technica AT95e cartridge → Radio Design Labs EZ-PH1 phono preamp → Focusrite Scarlett 2i2; Internet Archive VBR MP3 access derivative
fields.note: The stated lineage and digital formats are documented. The source-side file records SoX processing, but detailed settings, restoration, noise reduction, pitch correction and edits are not established. No such treatment is inferred from the sound or carrier-condition grade.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Debussy died in 1918 and the suite was published in 1908. This is territorial term reasoning for the composition, not worldwide clearance or a claim about an unidentified modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — EU public-domain term basis for a phonogram published before 1963; territorial, not worldwide.
fields.note: The documented LP issue is dated 1951, establishing publication before 1963 independently of the 1950 session. Its earlier 50-year phonogram term had expired before the 1 November 2013 extension threshold. US sound-recording status is not established. No Creative Commons licence or worldwide public-domain dedication is claimed.

composer.epithet: He trusted his ear over the rules — “pleasure is the law” — and made the piano, the flute and the orchestra sound new.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and went to prison for it, and there he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

His teachers could not make him out. Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, found “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament” in January 1874; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Years later, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud around 1890, he put his position plainly: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
